title: System Design in a Hurry — Quiz
subtitle: 40 questions covering all key technologies. Shuffled each attempt.

questions.q: Which type of database is generally recommended for product design system design interviews?
questions.exp: Relational databases are the default choice for product design interviews, while NoSQL is preferred for infrastructure design interviews.

questions.q: Which of the following is a yellow flag in a system design interview?
opts: Explaining the ACID properties of Postgres
Saying 'I need NoSQL because I need scale and performance'
questions.exp: Broad statements like 'I need NoSQL for scale' reveal inexperience — relational databases also scale incredibly well when used correctly.

questions.q: A candidate says 'I need a relational DB because I have relationships in my data.' Why is this a yellow flag?
opts: Relational databases don't support foreign keys
NoSQL databases can also handle relational data well, making this an oversimplification
NoSQL databases are always faster than relational databases
Relational databases can't scale beyond a single node
questions.exp: This is a yellow flag because NoSQL databases handle relational data well too. The statement reveals inexperience with broad generalizations rather than specific, context-driven reasoning.

questions.q: What feature allows combining data from multiple tables in a relational database?
questions.exp: SQL Joins combine data from multiple tables. They're powerful but can be a major performance bottleneck, so you should minimize them where possible.

questions.q: What data structures are indexes most commonly implemented with?
questions.exp: Relational database indexes are most commonly implemented using B-Trees or Hash Tables.

questions.q: What is a transaction in the context of relational databases?
opts: A way to replicate data across nodes
A method to group multiple operations into a single atomic operation
A type of index for fast lookups
questions.exp: Transactions group multiple operations into a single atomic operation — either all succeed or all fail — preventing invalid data states.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a common NoSQL data model?
questions.exp: NoSQL databases come in key-value, document, column-family, and graph flavors. Relational tables are the domain of RDBMS, not NoSQL.

questions.q: What scaling technique do NoSQL databases commonly use to distribute data?
questions.exp: NoSQL databases scale horizontally using consistent hashing and/or sharding to distribute data across many servers.

questions.q: Which NoSQL database is considered a good choice specifically for write-heavy workloads?
questions.exp: Cassandra is a good choice for write-heavy workloads due to its append-only storage model, though it comes with some tradeoffs in functionality.

questions.q: Why should large binary files like videos and images NOT be stored directly in a traditional database?
opts: Databases can't handle binary data at all
It is both expensive and inefficient
Databases lack encryption for binary files
questions.exp: Storing large blobs in a traditional database is both expensive and inefficient. Blob storage services like S3 are specifically designed for this and are far more cost-effective.

questions.q: What is a presigned URL used for in a blob storage workflow?
opts: Granting temporary upload or download access to a blob
questions.exp: Presigned URLs grant temporary access to a blob — either for upload or download — without exposing permanent credentials.

questions.q: What is the correct typical setup when using blob storage alongside a core database?
opts: Store everything in blob storage and skip the database
Use the database as a pointer store (URL) for blobs in S3
Use the CDN as the primary storage layer
Store metadata in blob storage and blobs in the database
questions.exp: The standard pattern: a core database (Postgres/DynamoDB) holds pointers (URLs) to blobs in S3. This gives you fast indexed queries on metadata with cheap blob storage.

questions.q: What technique allows resuming a failed large-file upload and uploading in parallel?
questions.exp: Chunking (multipart upload) splits large files into smaller pieces, enabling parallel upload and resumption after failure. S3 supports this via its multipart upload API.

questions.q: Why is a LIKE '%search_term%' query problematic for full-text search at scale?
opts: It requires a full table scan and doesn't use an index
It can only match exact strings
questions.exp: LIKE queries require a full table scan — the database checks every record — making them slow and unscalable for large text datasets.

questions.q: What data structure do search-optimized databases use to make full-text search fast?
questions.exp: Inverted indexes map from words to the documents containing them, enabling instant lookup instead of scanning every document.

questions.q: What is 'stemming' in the context of search databases?
opts: Reducing words to their root form so variants match
questions.exp: Stemming reduces words to their root form — e.g. 'running' and 'runs' both reduce to 'run' — so different forms of the same word match.

questions.q: Which search database is considered the clear leader and is built on Apache Lucene?
questions.exp: Elasticsearch is the clear leader in search-optimized databases. It is distributed, RESTful, built on Apache Lucene, and used by companies like Netflix, Uber, and Yelp.

questions.q: What is fuzzy search and how is it typically implemented?
opts: Searching only within a specific field; implemented with inverted indexes
Finding results similar to the search term despite misspellings; using edit distance algorithms
Searching across multiple tables; using SQL joins
Finding results matching a regex pattern; using tokenization
questions.exp: Fuzzy search finds results similar to the query even with misspellings. It uses edit distance — the number of character changes needed to transform one word into another.

questions.q: What is the primary role of an API gateway in a microservice architecture?
opts: Routing incoming requests to the appropriate backend service
questions.exp: The API gateway sits in front of your system, routes requests to the right backend service, and handles cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and logging.

questions.q: Which of the following is a cross-cutting concern typically handled by an API gateway?
questions.exp: API gateways handle cross-cutting concerns including authentication, rate limiting, and logging — concerns that apply across many services.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a load balancer in a system design?
opts: Distributing traffic across multiple machines to avoid hotspots
questions.exp: Load balancers distribute traffic across multiple machines (horizontal scaling) to prevent any single machine from being overloaded.

questions.q: When should you prefer an L4 load balancer over an L7 load balancer?
opts: When you need to route traffic to multiple services
When you have persistent connections like WebSockets
When you need to inspect HTTP headers
When you want more flexible routing rules
questions.exp: L4 load balancers work at the transport layer and are preferred for persistent connections like WebSockets. L7 load balancers are better for flexible HTTP routing.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a queue in a system design?
opts: Serving as a buffer for bursty traffic and distributing work
questions.exp: Queues buffer bursty traffic (so requests aren't dropped) and distribute work across a pool of workers, smoothing load on the system.

questions.q: Why should you avoid adding a queue to a synchronous workload with strict latency requirements (e.g. <500ms)?
opts: Adding a queue nearly guarantees breaking that latency constraint
questions.exp: Queues introduce asynchrony. If you have strong latency SLAs, adding a queue will almost certainly violate them since messages wait before being processed.

questions.q: What is a dead letter queue used for?
opts: Storing the most recently processed messages
Storing messages that cannot be processed for debugging and auditing
Providing priority ordering to queue consumers
Holding messages during peak traffic spikes
questions.exp: Dead letter queues store messages that failed to be processed, enabling debugging and auditing to understand why they failed.

questions.q: What is backpressure in the context of queues?
opts: The lag between producer and consumer speed
Slowing or rejecting new messages when the queue is overwhelmed
questions.exp: Backpressure slows down message production when the queue is overwhelmed, preventing the system from being crushed by more requests than it can handle.

questions.q: What key capability distinguishes streams from traditional message queues?
opts: Streams are always faster than queues
Streams retain data for a configurable period, allowing consumers to re-read from past positions
Streams don't require a partition key
questions.exp: Unlike queues that delete messages after consumption, streams retain data for a configurable period, enabling consumers to replay or re-read from any past position.

questions.q: What is event sourcing?
opts: Emitting events when a cache is invalidated
Storing application state changes as a sequence of replayable events
Streaming video from blob storage via CDN
questions.exp: Event sourcing stores every state change as an event. These events can be replayed to reconstruct application state at any point in time — useful for audit trails and rollbacks.

questions.q: What is 'windowing' in the context of stream processing?
opts: Splitting a stream into multiple partitions
Grouping events together based on time or count for batch processing
Assigning consumer groups to stream partitions
Replicating stream data for fault tolerance
questions.exp: Windowing groups stream events by time or count — e.g. computing hourly delivery time averages — enabling batch-style aggregations over a continuous stream.

questions.q: What is the purpose of multiple consumer groups in a stream?
opts: To allow different consumers to process the same stream data independently for different purposes
To replicate the stream across data centers
To enforce message ordering across partitions
questions.exp: Multiple consumer groups let different downstream processors independently consume the same stream — e.g. one group updates a dashboard while another writes to a DB for historical analysis.

questions.q: Why are standard database transaction locks insufficient for scenarios like temporarily holding a concert ticket for a user?
opts: Transaction locks don't support key-value data
Transaction locks are not designed for longer-term locking across systems
Transaction locks are too slow for web applications
questions.exp: Database transaction locks ensure consistency during a single operation but aren't designed for longer-term, cross-system locking like holding a ticket for 10 minutes while a user checks out.

questions.q: What is a key feature of distributed locks that prevents them from getting stuck indefinitely if a process crashes?
questions.exp: Distributed locks can be set to expire after a certain time (TTL). If the process that acquired the lock crashes, the lock auto-releases after the TTL.

questions.q: What is a deadlock in the context of distributed locks?
opts: A situation where a lock is acquired by two processes simultaneously
A situation where two processes wait for each other to release locks, causing both to stall forever
A lock that expires before the operation completes
A lock held across too many partitions
questions.exp: Deadlocks occur when process A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while process B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1 — both stall indefinitely.

questions.q: Which of the following is a valid reason to use a distributed cache?
opts: To reduce the number of expensive database queries
questions.exp: Caches reduce DB load by storing results of expensive queries in memory for fast retrieval, avoiding redundant computation or DB hits.

questions.q: What does the LRU eviction policy do?
opts: Removes items in the order they were added
Removes the item accessed least frequently
Removes the item that was accessed least recently
Removes items randomly when the cache is full
questions.exp: LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the item that hasn't been accessed for the longest time, keeping frequently accessed items in cache.

questions.q: What is a write-back cache?
opts: Writes data simultaneously to the cache and the datastore
Writes data directly to the datastore, bypassing the cache
Writes data to the cache first, then asynchronously writes to the datastore
Only writes to the cache and never persists to disk
questions.exp: Write-back (write-behind) caches write to the cache first and flush to the datastore asynchronously. Faster writes, but risk of data loss if the cache fails before flushing.

questions.q: Which two technologies are the most common in-memory distributed caches?
questions.exp: Redis and Memcached are the dominant in-memory caches. Redis supports rich data structures (sorted sets, lists, etc.); Memcached is simpler.

questions.q: How does a CDN deliver content to users quickly across the globe?
opts: By replicating the entire database to every region
By caching content on servers geographically close to users (edge locations)
By compressing responses at the origin server
By using L4 load balancers to route globally
questions.exp: CDNs cache content at edge servers geographically near users. Requests hit the nearest edge, reducing latency. Only cache misses go back to the origin.

questions.q: What type of content can CDNs cache beyond just static assets?
questions.exp: CDNs can cache dynamic content like API responses, not just static assets. This is especially useful for content accessed frequently but changing infrequently.

questions.q: In a blob storage workflow, what role does a CDN typically play?
opts: A caching layer in front of blob storage to serve files from edge locations
A queue to handle upload bursts
A distributed lock for concurrent uploads
questions.exp: The CDN sits in front of blob storage (S3 acts as origin). Files are cached at edge locations globally, so users download from a nearby edge server, not the origin.
